newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eramet to hold N.Caledonia talks as pressure mounts.
newsitem.headline: Eramet to hold N.Caledonia talks as pressure mounts.

text.p: Eramet, the world's third largest nickel producer, said on Wednesday it will meet with the management of Canadian group Falconbridge and Societe Miniere du Sud Pacifique (SMSP) on Friday to discuss their plans to build a rival nickel plant in New Caledonia.

But the news came as the majority shareholder, state- controlled holding Erap, sharply criticised the way Eramet's managers had handled a long-standing dispute over the distribution of mining assets in the French territory.
"In this affair we blame Eramet's managers for having wasted an enormous amount of time," Erap chairman Remy Chardon told French daily La Tribune.

Chardon said that an agreement over mining assets was a priority but that it would be difficult for Eramet's management to participate in the talks, adding to speculation that Eramet chairman Yves Rambaud might soon be replaced.

Eramet has repeatedly said it was supporting plans by Canadian group Falconbridge and local Kanak company SMSP to build a nickel plant in the north of the South Pacific island as long as it did not threaten its development strategy in New Caledonia.
Rambaud has also repeatedly said that all industrial players involved must discuss the fate of the plant. He offered last week to meet with the presidents of Falconbridge and SMSP.
Eramet has said it is ready to help supply the northern plant and also participate in an initial plan to swap mines wih SMSP as long as the exchange was fair.
But it has opposed a plan by government to withdraw Eramet's licence for the Koniambo field to hand it to SMSP and Falconbridge, as this would curb Eramet's development in New Caledonia.
Goverment decided to withdraw the Koniambo licence after talks over an initial plan to swap mining assets failed.
Government support of the new smelter is aimed at appeasing Kanak separatists ahead of a 1998 referendum on independence for the French territory.

Industry sources said Friday's meeting was likely to focus on the initial plan to swap mining assets and possible compensation that would be paid to Eramet if the exchange took place. Talks might also clarify several issues including how much ore was needed to supply the new plant and how much SMPS and Eramet could provide.
The meeting might also provide more details on the cost of the smelter and Falconbridge's plans, they said.
But Friday's meeting looked very much like a last chance for Rambaud, whose hard-line stand has irked government, they added.
Erap, which controls 55 percent of Eramet, has said it wants to appoint a majority of the directors on Eramet's board.
If shareholders approve the motion at a May 29 meeting, this could pave the way for Rambaud's ouster.
"Erap would like to have an outright majority when Eramet's board is renewed," Chardon said. "The arrival of new men at the head of Eramet will help take some heat out of the conflict."

But the ouster of Rambaud, who is highly regarded by investors and analysts, will not go down well with minority shareholders, notably pension funds, who have been sharply critical of the government role in the conflict.
